title: Soviet Caucasus
subtitle: 1921–1953 · The Transcaucasian Federation, Autonomies and Borders, the Terror, the War and the Deportations

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The party leaders of the republics, Beria's Georgia, Baghirov's Azerbaijan and the Armenian secretaries, under Moscow

entries.label: The Armenian party secretaries
entries.hint: Armenia's party was led by Aghasi Khanjian (1930–1936), who died in Beria's office in 1936, Amatuni (1936–1937) and Grigory Arutinov (1937–1953), under Moscow's watch; Arutinov guided the republic through the Terror, the war and the repatriation of the diaspora.
entries.note: Ronald Suny, Looking toward Ararat (1993); Richard Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People, vol. 2 (1997).

entries.label: Ordzhonikidze and Kirov
entries.hint: Sergo Ordzhonikidze, a Georgian Bolshevik, ran the Caucasian Bureau and the Transcaucasian party in the early 1920s, and Sergei Kirov was first secretary of the Azerbaijani party from 1921 to 1926 and the champion of the oil industry; they were the first generation of Soviet governors of the region before the Stalinist cadres.

entries.label: Lavrenti Beria
entries.hint: Lavrenti Beria, a Mingrelian from the Sukhumi district and former Chekist, was head of the Georgian Communist party from 1931 and of the Transcaucasian party from 1932, in charge of the republic through the collectivisation and the Terror, and when he moved to Moscow in 1938 to head the NKVD he took the Georgian cadres with him.
entries.note: Amy Knight, Beria: Stalin's First Lieutenant (1993); Suny 1994.

entries.label: Mir Jafar Baghirov
entries.hint: Mir Jafar Baghirov, a former Chekist, was first secretary of the Azerbaijan Communist party from 1933 to 1953, ruled with harshness in the purge of the 1930s and the oil war economy, and, after Stalin's death and Beria's fall in 1953, was arrested and shot in 1956; he is a symbol of the Stalinist age.
entries.note: Audrey Altstadt, The Azerbaijani Turks (1992); Tadeusz Swietochowski, Russian Azerbaijan (1985).

entries.label: The Transcaucasian Federation
entries.hint: In March 1922 Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan were united in the Transcaucasian Federation, which entered the USSR as one republic, the TSFSR, on 30 December 1922; it was run from Tbilisi by a Communist party committee under Moscow's Caucasian Bureau and was dissolved in December 1936 when each republic became a Union republic.
entries.note: Ronald Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1994); Terry Martin, The Affirmative Action Empire (2001).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Georgian rising of 1924, the Terror of 1937–1938, the Battle of the Caucasus and the arrests of 1949–1951

entries.label: The August rising in Georgia
entries.hint: In August 1924 a planned rising of Georgian nationalist and Menshevik groups, the Committee for Independence, broke out in Chiatura, Guria, Mingrelia and other regions; the Red Army and the Cheka crushed it in a few days, and in the following weeks of repression several thousand people were shot or deported; the numbers are put at between about 3,000 and 10,000.
entries.note: Suny 1994; Georgian archive documents; Zhordania's circle.

entries.label: The Great Terror
entries.hint: In 1937–1938 the NKVD arrested tens of thousands in each republic, the party leaders, intellectuals, clergy and others, charged them with spying and conspiracy, and shot many thousands: the Georgian writers Mikheil Javakhishvili and Titsian Tabidze were shot in 1937, Paolo Iashvili killed himself, Yeghishe Charents of Armenia died in prison in 1937, and in Azerbaijan Mikayil Mushfig and Huseyn Javid were destroyed.

entries.label: The war effort of the republics
entries.hint: Hundreds of thousands of Georgians, Armenians and Azerbaijanis served in the Red Army, among them some 700,000 Georgians (with approximately 300,000 dead), about half a million Armenians and some 600,000 Azerbaijanis, and their republics' mines, mills and above all Baku's oil supplied the war; the Armenian marshals Baghramyan and Khudyakov and Admiral Isakov are named.

entries.label: The Battle of the Caucasus
entries.hint: In the summer of 1942 the German army group A under List and Kleist, in Operation Edelweiss, advanced into the North Caucasus towards the oil of Maikop, Grozny and Baku; German mountain troops raised a flag on Mount Elbrus in August, but the advance was halted short of the Transcaucasian passes by the Soviet defence in the Terek and Mozdok, and the Germans withdrew by January 1943.
entries.note: Soviet and German war histories; Antony Beevor, Stalingrad (1998).

entries.label: Pishevari and the claims on Kars and Ardahan
entries.loc: Soviet Azerbaijan, Iranian Azerbaijan and Kars
entries.hint: In 1945–1946 the Soviet leadership under Stalin, with Baghirov as its manager, backed the creation of an Azerbaijan People's Government in the Iranian province of Azerbaijan under Jafar Pishevari, until the Red Army withdrew in 1946; and in 1945 Moscow demanded from Turkey the return of Kars and Ardahan and bases on the Straits, a pressure which helped bring Turkey to NATO.
entries.note: Soviet and Iranian documents; Swietochowski 1985; Altstadt 1992.

entries.label: The Mingrelian affair and the arrests of 1949–1951
entries.hint: In 1951–1952 Stalin and the security chief Abakumov engineered in Georgia a purge of Mingrelian officials, Beria's clients, in which hundreds were arrested; in 1949 tens of thousands of people in the three republics, Greeks, Turks, Dashnak families and others, among them some returned repatriates, were deported to Siberia and Kazakhstan on suspicion of unreliability.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Federation, the autonomies of Karabakh, Nakhchivan, Abkhazia and South Ossetia, the constitutions of 1936 and the script changes

entries.label: The autonomous territories
entries.loc: Karabakh, Nakhchivan, Abkhazia and South Ossetia
entries.hint: In the Soviet settlement Moscow created, within the republics, units of autonomy: the Adjara ASSR (1921) and the Abkhaz SSR (1921; an autonomous republic within Georgia from 1931), the South Ossetian autonomous oblast (April 1922), the Nakhchivan ASSR (1924) under Azerbaijan and the Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous oblast (July 1923) in Azerbaijan, with a majority of Armenians, and the shifting of Zangezur to Armenia. The origins of later conflicts lie here.
entries.note: Decrees of the Caucasian Bureau and TsIK (1921–1924); Suny 1994; Martin 2001.

entries.label: The Georgian affair
entries.hint: In 1922 Stalin and Sergo Ordzhonikidze pressed Georgia's Communist leaders, Budu Mdivani and Pilipe Makharadze, to enter a Transcaucasian federation rather than join the USSR directly; the Georgian leaders resisted and were removed, an incident in which Ordzhonikidze struck an opponent, and Lenin, ill, wrote in his last letters of 'great-Russian chauvinism' and urged Stalin's removal.
entries.note: Lenin, 'On the national question' (30–31 December 1922); Suny 1994.

entries.label: Korenizatsiia, the policy of rooting
entries.hint: The Soviet policy of korenizatsiia or indigenisation, adopted in 1923, promoted native languages, cadres and culture in the republics, with schools, newspapers and publishing in Georgian, Armenian and Azerbaijani and the promotion of local people in the party and administration; it was curtailed by the early 1930s.
entries.note: Resolutions of the XII Party Congress (1923); Terry Martin, The Affirmative Action Empire (2001).

entries.label: The change of scripts
entries.hint: Azerbaijan adopted the Latin alphabet in 1929 in place of Arabic script, following a Turkic-wide movement, and in 1939–1940 the Soviets replaced it with a Cyrillic alphabet, cutting the republic off from Turkey and from its own earlier press; Georgian and Armenian scripts were kept.

entries.label: The constitutions of 1936
entries.hint: The Soviet constitution of 5 December 1936 dissolved the Transcaucasian Federation and gave each of the three republics the status of a Union republic with its own supreme soviet; it was followed by republican constitutions in 1937, which in form gave the republics the right of secession but not in practice.
entries.note: Constitution of the USSR (5 December 1936); Suny 1994.

entries.label: The end of Mingrelian and Svan literacy
entries.hint: Mingrelian and Svan, the two languages of the Kartvelian family spoken in western Georgia, had been developed as written languages with schools and newspapers in the 1930s, but in 1938 the Soviet authorities abolished their schools and publications and the languages were subordinated to Georgian; the measure was part of the nationality policy of the Terror.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The closing of churches and mosques, the murdered catholicos and the wartime concordat

entries.label: The Terror against the churches
entries.hint: In Georgia the Catholicos Ambrosi was arrested in 1923 for protesting to the Genoa Conference, and by the end of the 1930s most monasteries and churches were closed; in Armenia the Catholicos Khoren I died under suspicious circumstances in 1938, the Etchmiadzin treasury was seized, and the seat was vacant until 1945.

entries.label: Islam under the anti-religious campaign
entries.hint: The Soviet authorities closed or converted most of Azerbaijan's mosques and madrasas, with the banning of Muharram processions, the end of waqf property and the arrest or execution of clergy, as a part of the campaign against religion and the veil; the republic had only a few mosques left by the war.

entries.label: The wartime concordat
entries.hint: After Stalin's accommodation of the Russian church in 1943, the Moscow Patriarchate recognised the autocephaly of the Georgian church in 1943, a relationship repaired; in Armenia Gevorg VI was elected Catholicos in 1945 with Stalin's consent, and the church was allowed some functioning and contact with the diaspora.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Yerevan plan, Khachaturian and Hajibeyov, Georgian cinema and the writers of the Terror

entries.label: Georgian cinema and the writers
entries.hint: Georgian film studios produced in the 1920s and 1930s the works of Kote Marjanishvili, Nikoloz Shengelaia and Mikheil Kalatozishvili (Kalatozov, 'Salt for Svanetia', 1930), and in the 1940s the official epics of Mikheil Chiaureli, including 'The Vow' (1946) and 'The Fall of Berlin' (1949), glorifying Stalin; writers such as Konstantine Gamsakhurdia and Grigol Robakidze (an emigré from 1931) made names.

entries.label: Tamanian's Yerevan
entries.hint: Alexander Tamanian, an architect who had returned from Russia, drew in 1924 a plan for Yerevan on a circular and radial scheme, with Republic Square and a long axis, and built the opera house, government house and others in neoclassical forms from pink tuff; the plan made Yerevan a modern capital.
entries.note: Tamanian's master plan (1924); Armenian architectural surveys.

entries.label: Khachaturian and Hajibeyov
entries.hint: Aram Khachaturian (1903–1978), born in Tbilisi, composed the Piano Concerto (1936), the ballet 'Gayane' (1942) with the 'Sabre Dance', and the Violin Concerto; Uzeyir Hajibeyov wrote the opera 'Koroglu' (1937) and the operetta 'Arshin Mal Alan' (1913, filmed in 1945), the music of the national schools.

entries.label: The jubilees of Rustaveli and Nizami
entries.hint: The Soviet state, which had adopted a policy of national heritage within a socialist form, celebrated the 750th anniversary of Rustaveli in 1937 and the 800th of Nizami in 1947 with editions, museums and monuments, while the same years saw the repression of living writers; the jubilees helped to shape official national canons.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The academies and observatories, the nationality theory and the historians under watch

entries.label: Marr, Javakhishvili and Soviet historiography
entries.hint: The linguist Nikolai Marr, with his Japhetic theory claiming a common origin for the Caucasian languages and then a stadial theory of language, was the official doctrine in Soviet linguistics until Stalin condemned it in 1950; the Georgian historian Ivane Javakhishvili (1876–1940), founder of Tbilisi University, published a history of the Georgian nation, and Soviet historians of the three republics wrote under party control.
entries.note: Marr, Japhetic studies; Javakhishvili, History of the Georgian Nation; Stalin, Marxism and Linguistics (1950).

entries.label: The academies and Byurakan
entries.hint: The Georgian Academy of Sciences was founded in 1941, the Armenian in 1943 under Hovsep Orbeli and the Azerbaijan Academy in 1945, with the Byurakan Astrophysical Observatory, founded in 1946 by Viktor Ambartsumian near Yerevan, which became one of the leading observatories of the Soviet Union.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Baku's oil in the war, collectivisation, Rustavi and the Sevan–Hrazdan hydropower

entries.label: Baku's oil in the Soviet economy and the war
entries.hint: Nationalised in 1920, Baku's oil returned to its pre-war levels by the late 1920s and was the main source of Soviet oil, giving more than two-thirds of the USSR's output on the eve of the war, in 1941 some 23.5 million tonnes, which fuelled the Red Army; the Soviet government planned to blow up the wells in 1942 if the Germans came.

entries.label: Tea, citrus and subtropical farming
entries.hint: With drainage of the Colchian marshes and the planting of tea and citrus groves in Adjara, Guria and Abkhazia, Georgia became the Soviet Union's main producer of tea and citrus fruit, with large collective and state farms; the Colchis lowland was transformed in the 1930s and 1940s.

entries.label: Collectivisation and the villages
entries.hint: The forced collectivisation of 1929–1931 and later met resistance in Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan: peasant risings in Guria, Svaneti and Kakheti, in Zangezur and in Muslim mountain districts were put down by the army; the kulaks were deported, and the collectives specialised in cotton in Azerbaijan, tea and citrus in Georgia and vines and fruit in Armenia.

entries.label: Rustavi and the Sevan–Hrazdan cascade
entries.hint: Industrialisation brought the Zestafoni ferroalloy and Rustavi iron and steel works in Georgia (from 1944), the Kirovakan chemical works and hydropower on the Hrazdan in Armenia and the lowering of Lake Sevan for power, a plan that cut its level by more than twenty metres in the following decades.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The hydropower cascade, the pipelines and the radio telescope

entries.label: Hydropower and the Sevan scheme
entries.hint: The Zemo Avchala (1927) and Rioni (1933) plants in Georgia and the Hrazdan–Sevan cascade in Armenia, begun in the 1930s, provided the electricity of the republics; the Sevan scheme, which diverted the lake's waters through tunnels, was one of the main Soviet water projects.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Armenian repatriation of 1946–1949 and the Lend-Lease route through Iran

entries.label: The Persian corridor and Lend-Lease
entries.hint: After the Anglo-Soviet occupation of Iran in August 1941, Allied supplies, trucks and aircraft reached the USSR by the Persian Gulf, Iran's railway and Caspian ports, passing through Baku and the Transcaucasian railway; the route was one of the main channels of Lend-Lease aid.

entries.label: The Armenian repatriation
entries.hint: In response to Stalin's call in 1945, some 90,000 to 100,000 Armenians from Syria, Lebanon, Iran, Greece, France, the United States and elsewhere moved to Soviet Armenia in 1946–1949, hoping to build the homeland; most were housed in poor conditions, treated with suspicion, and some were arrested or deported in 1949.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The famine of 1930s and the war losses

entries.label: Famine and war losses
entries.hint: Collectivisation and the war brought shortages and famine in Armenia and Azerbaijan in some years; the republics lost heavily in the war, about 300,000 of Georgia's soldiers, and the Terror took many more; the three populations nevertheless rose from about 6 million in 1926 to nearly 9 million in 1959.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The unveiling campaign, the Meskhetian deportation and the families of the Terror

entries.label: The unveiling campaign
entries.hint: The Soviet 'Hujum' (assault), a campaign to end the veil in Muslim regions, led in Azerbaijan in 1927–1929 to public unveilings, the banning of the veil by party members' wives and the opening of women's clubs and schools; it met resistance, and women who unveiled were attacked and sometimes murdered.

entries.label: The families of the Terror
entries.hint: The families of those arrested, children, wives and parents, lost homes and jobs, were sent to labour camps or exile in Kazakhstan, and for many years kept silent about the fates of their relatives; the lists of the victims have been recovered by memorial groups since the 1990s.

entries.label: The Meskhetian deportation
entries.hint: On 14–15 November 1944 the NKVD deported by train to Central Asia some 90,000 to 115,000 Meskhetian Turks, with Kurds and Hemshin Armenians, from the border districts of Meskheti-Javakheti in Georgia, officially for the security of the frontier; thousands died on the way and in exile, and as of 2026 only part of the community has been able to return.
entries.note: GKO decree no. 6279 (31 July 1944); Suny 1994; J. Otto Pohl, Ethnic Cleansing in the USSR (1999).
